_about: Explanations written for this website, shared by all proceedings papers. 'match' lists exact spellings to underline (case-sensitive, whole words). Not part of the proceedings.

terms.def: Orbits up to roughly 2,000 km above the Earth, where the International Space Station and most Earth-observation and communication constellations fly. Satellites there circle the Earth in about 90 to 120 minutes.
An orbit about 36,000 km above the equator in which a satellite turns with the Earth, so it appears fixed in the sky. Weather and communication satellites often use it.
The region between geostationary orbit and the Moon. Objects there are far away and faint, which makes them hard to track.
Estimating where a satellite is and how it moves from measurements such as ranges, angles or GNSS positions, using a model of the forces acting on it.
Global Navigation Satellite Systems: GPS, Galileo, GLONASS and BeiDou. Receivers on satellites can use them to measure their own position.
A close approach between two objects in orbit. Operators receive Conjunction Data Messages with updated estimates of the risk and decide whether to move a satellite.
Knowing what is in orbit, where it is and where it is going, to avoid collisions and understand the space environment.
Missions that capture or de-orbit pieces of space debris to reduce collision risk.
Repairing, refuelling or inspecting satellites in orbit, usually with a robotic servicer spacecraft.
A spacecraft's orientation in space: which way it is pointing. Attitude control keeps it pointing the right way.
The onboard functions that decide where a spacecraft should go (guidance), work out where it is (navigation) and steer it there (control).
A spinning wheel inside a spacecraft. Speeding it up or slowing it down turns the spacecraft the other way, without using fuel.
A fast-spinning wheel that is tilted to produce large turning forces, used to rotate larger spacecraft quickly.
A system with fewer independent controls than directions it can move in, for example a spacecraft that cannot directly push around one of its axes.
Fault Detection, Isolation and Recovery: the onboard logic that notices something is wrong, finds the cause and puts the spacecraft back in a safe state.
The measurements a spacecraft sends to the ground about its own state, such as temperatures, voltages and positions, usually as many time series.
Automatically spotting data that do not look like normal behaviour, for example a sensor reading that signals a developing fault.
The main computer of a spacecraft that runs its software.
Sending data from a spacecraft to the ground. Bandwidth and contact time are limited, which is why deciding onboard what to send is valuable.
Everything on Earth that operates a mission: antennas, control centres and data processing.
A bit in electronic memory flipped by a charged particle from space radiation. It can silently corrupt data or a neural network's weights.
Electronics designed and tested to survive space radiation and temperature swings. They are reliable but usually much slower than consumer chips.
Commercial off-the-shelf: ordinary commercial components, cheaper and faster than space-qualified ones but less tested for space.
Field-Programmable Gate Array: a chip whose circuits can be reconfigured after manufacture, popular in space for fast, low-power custom processing.
A single chip that combines processors, memory interfaces and often an FPGA or accelerator.
An open instruction-set standard for processors, increasingly used in European space-grade chips.
Ways to do the same operation on several numbers at once. SWAR packs several small numbers into one register, which speeds up low-precision neural networks.
Storing a neural network's numbers with fewer bits, for example 8-bit integers instead of 32-bit floats. It saves memory, time and power, sometimes at a small cost in accuracy.
Removing parts of a neural network (weights, neurons or channels) that contribute little, to make it smaller and faster.
Counts of arithmetic operations a model needs. A rough indicator of computing cost, though real run time also depends on the hardware.
Running a trained model on new data to get predictions, as opposed to training it.
Processing data where it is collected (here: on the spacecraft) instead of sending it elsewhere first.
Imaging and measuring the Earth from space, for example for maps, agriculture, disasters or climate.
Satellites of Europe's Copernicus programme. Sentinel-1 carries radar that sees through clouds; Sentinel-2 takes optical images in 13 colour bands.
A radar imaging technique that works day and night and through clouds by combining echoes collected as the satellite moves.
Images with several (multispectral) or hundreds (hyperspectral) of colour bands, many invisible to the eye, that reveal materials and gases.
Nadir is straight down. Off-nadir imaging means the satellite looks sideways, which lets it revisit places more often but distorts the view.
Correcting a satellite image for terrain and viewing angle so it lines up with a map. Usually done on the ground.
Producing a sharper image than the sensor captured, using a model that has learned what fine detail usually looks like.
Comparing images of the same place at different times to find what changed.
Labelling every pixel of an image with a class, such as water, ship or rock.
Finding objects in an image and drawing a box around each one.
Working out an object's position and orientation (pose) from images, for example another spacecraft's position relative to the camera.
A camera whose pixels report changes in brightness as they happen instead of full frames, giving very fast, low-power motion sensing.
How a telescope spreads the light of a single point source, such as a star, across the image.
A planet orbiting a star other than the Sun.
A star's brightness measured over time. A small regular dip can mean a planet passing in front of it.
A 3D simulation of a planet's atmosphere: winds, temperatures and pressure all around the planet. Accurate but slow to compute.
A point mass used to model an irregular body's gravity field: many mascons together mimic the body's uneven mass distribution.
A model made of layers of simple units with adjustable weights, trained on examples to map inputs to outputs.
A neural network built for images: it slides small learned filters across the image to detect patterns.
A widely used CNN design for segmentation that first shrinks the image to understand it, then expands it back to label every pixel.
A neural network design built on attention. It powers large language models and, as vision transformers (ViT), image models.
A mechanism that lets a model weigh which parts of its input matter most for each output.
Neural networks for sequences that carry a memory from one time step to the next. LSTM and GRU are common variants that remember longer.
The simplest neural network: a few fully connected layers.
A network trained to compress its input into a few numbers and reconstruct it. Inputs it reconstructs badly are unusual, which is useful for anomaly detection.
The compressed internal representation a model builds, where similar inputs end up close together.
A large model pre-trained on huge, broad datasets that can be reused for many tasks with little or no extra training.
A very large transformer trained on text that can answer questions, summarise and generate text.
A language model that first looks up relevant passages in a document collection and then answers using them.
Facts stored as a network of entities and the relations between them, which a computer can query.
A formal vocabulary that defines the kinds of things in a domain and how they relate.
Learning by trial and error: an agent acts, receives rewards, and gradually learns which actions pay off.
The standard mathematical description of a sequential decision problem used in reinforcement learning: states, actions, transitions and rewards.
A widely used, stable reinforcement-learning algorithm.
A learned model of how the environment responds to actions, which an agent can use to imagine outcomes before acting.
A neural network trained not only to fit data but also to obey known physical equations, which helps when data are scarce.
A network with a random, fixed hidden layer where only the output weights are fitted, often in one step. Very fast to train.
A neural network that describes how a system changes over time, solved with standard differential-equation solvers, so it can be combined with known physics.
A neural network that represents a 3D scene so it can be rendered from any viewpoint, learned from ordinary images.
A fast learned approximation of a slow simulation.
A detailed simulation of a real system that is kept in step with it, used to predict or explain its behaviour.
Pre-training a model on unlabelled data by giving it a task built from the data itself, such as recognising two altered versions of the same image as the same.
Starting from a model already trained on one task and adapting it to another with less data.
A loop in which the model picks the examples it is least sure about for a human to label, so labelling effort goes where it helps most.
Updating a model continuously as new data arrive, instead of training it once.
When the data a model sees slowly change over time, so a model trained once becomes less accurate.
Data that differ from what a model was trained on. Models are often unreliable on such data.
The difference between training data (often synthetic) and real data that makes models perform worse in reality.
Artificially generated data, for example rendered images or simulated telemetry, used when real data are scarce.
Estimating how unsure a model is about each prediction, so users know when not to trust it.
A method that turns any model's outputs into prediction sets or intervals with a statistical guarantee of containing the true answer a chosen share of the time.
Running a network several times with random parts switched off to see how much its predictions vary, as a cheap uncertainty estimate.
A statistical model that predicts a smooth function and gives an error bar for every prediction.
A matrix describing how uncertain several estimated quantities are and how their errors are related.
Statistics of rare, extreme values, used here to set alarm thresholds that control false alarms.
Ways to measure prediction error: the average squared difference (MSE), its square root (RMSE), or the average absolute difference (MAE). Lower is better.
Precision: of everything flagged, the share that was correct. Recall: of everything that should have been flagged, the share that was found.
A single number combining precision and recall (their harmonic mean). F0.5 weighs precision more, for when false alarms are costly.
Area under the ROC curve: how well a detector ranks positives above negatives across all thresholds. 1 is perfect, 0.5 is guessing.
Intersection over union: how well a predicted region overlaps the true one. 1 means a perfect match.
Structural similarity index: a measure of how similar two images look, from 0 to 1.
Removing one part of a method at a time to see how much each part contributes.
A standard dataset and scoring procedure for comparing methods fairly.
Methods that show why a model made a prediction, for example which pixels or inputs mattered most.
Designing complex systems such as satellites with formal models instead of documents. SysML is its standard modelling language.
The European Union's law regulating artificial intelligence, with extra obligations, such as human oversight, for high-risk systems.
The European Space Agency.
ESA's technical centre in Noordwijk, the Netherlands, where SPAICE 2026 took place.
Space telescopes that find exoplanets by watching stars dim. TESS (NASA) is operating; PLATO (ESA) is due to launch.
ESA's space telescope mapping billions of galaxies to study dark matter and dark energy.
A planned ESA mission that will study the atmospheres of about 1,000 exoplanets.
The European–Russian, now European-led, Mars programme whose Rosalind Franklin rover will drill for signs of past life.
The Low-Frequency Array, a large European radio telescope network that also records radio bursts from the Sun.
Conditions in near-Earth space driven by the Sun, such as energetic particles, that can damage electronics and endanger astronauts.
